An offering divides work between the giver and the priests

The chapter splits the work between two parties. The giver brings the animal, lays a hand on it, kills it, and washes it. The priests handle only the blood and the altar fire. Verse 4 ties the hand on its head to being “accepted for him.” So the offering is the giver’s own act, not a show he watches. A bull, a sheep, or a bird are all allowed (verses 3, 10, and 14). Each gets the same closing words: a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
An ordinary food gift also supports sacred work

Flour, oil, and salt are kitchen goods, not herd animals. So this offering comes from daily bread. Verse 2 has the priest burn only a handful. Verse 3 gives the rest to Aaron and his sons. The gift to God is also the priests’ food, and it is called “most holy.” Priests had no fields of their own to harvest (Numbers 18:20–21). So a household’s bread helped keep the tent’s workers fed.
A shared offering still places limits on consumption

Chapter 7:15 shows that the giver ate meat from a peace offering. So this is a shared meal, unlike the burnt offering of chapter 1. Chapter 3 says what is held back from the table. The fat is burned, and verse 16 says, “all the fat is the LORD’s.” The blood goes on the altar. Verse 17 turns that into a lasting rule “in all your dwellings.” Even a feast with God keeps some parts that are not for the eater.
An error by a leader can involve a wider community

The chapter sorts offerings by who sinned. A priest or the whole assembly brings a bull (verses 3 and 14). A ruler brings a male goat, and a common person a female goat or lamb. The size of the animal follows the reach of the person’s role. Verse 3 says why: the priest’s sin brings guilt on the people. For priest and assembly the blood is taken inside the tent (verses 6 and 17). The assembly, ruler, and common person each end forgiven (verses 20, 26, 31).
Access to worship includes those with less

Verse 6 sets the normal offering at a lamb or goat. Verse 7 opens a second door for someone who “can’t afford a lamb.” Verse 11 opens a third: a small measure of flour. Each level ends with the same words: atonement, and “he will be forgiven.” So the price changes with the person’s means, and the result does not. Verse 5 asks one thing of everyone first: to confess. Verse 16 adds repayment plus a fifth where something was taken.
Repair reaches the person whose property was taken

Verse 2 calls cheating a neighbor “a trespass against the LORD.” So a wrong against a person is also a wrong against God. Verse 5 deals with the person first. The item goes back in full, plus a fifth, to “him to whom it belongs.” It must happen the day guilt is found, not later. Only then does verse 6 bring the ram to the priest. Forgiveness in verse 7 follows repair, and does not replace it.
A thanksgiving offering creates food that cannot be kept indefinitely

A whole animal is more meat than one family can eat in a day. Verse 15 says none of the thanksgiving meat may be left until morning. So the giver would need others to help eat it. The meat cannot be stored up as private stock. Verses 16–18 allow one more day for vows and free gifts, then require burning. Verse 14 gives a share of the bread to the priest. Thanks to God is shown here by a table that others eat from.
The community witnesses the beginning of priestly authority

Exodus 29 gave these steps as orders. Here Moses carries them out one by one. Verse 3 adds where: in front of “all the congregation.” The people see Aaron washed, dressed, and anointed. So his office is not a private claim. Everyone knows who made him priest and how. The phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” keeps returning (verses 9, 13, 17, 21, 29).
The priest must address his own need before serving others

Verse 7 gives the order: his own sin offering first, then the people’s. Verse 8 says the calf “was for himself.” Aaron made the gold calf in Exodus 32:4. His first offering is a calf. The priest stands with the people as someone who also needs atonement. Only after both offerings does he bless them (verse 22). The fire in verse 24 shows the offerings were accepted.
Grief creates a question within the prescribed service

Aaron has lost two sons that day and may not mourn (verses 6–7). The rule was that priests eat the sin offering (6:26). Aaron’s remaining sons burned it, and Moses is angry (verses 16–18). Aaron answers with a question in verse 19. After “such things as these,” would eating it have pleased the LORD? He does not claim a rule; he asks what fits the day. Verse 20 says Moses was satisfied, and the chapter ends there.
Temporary uncleanness requires a process rather than a moral verdict

Verse 40 is about an animal Israel may eat that dies by itself. Someone has to move the body. The verse does not forbid it or call it sin. It says to wash clothes and wait until evening. So “unclean” here is a short state with a simple way out. It limits contact with holy things for a time. Verses 44–45 give the reason for the rules: “be holy; for I am holy.”
Childbirth rules govern access without accusing the mother of a crime

The chapter does not say the mother did wrong. Genesis 1:28 commands people to be fruitful. Her state comes from the blood of birth, as verses 4 and 7 say. It keeps her from holy things and the sanctuary for a set time. Verse 8 lowers the cost for a poor family, as 5:7 did. The result is the same either way: “she shall be clean.” Luke 2:22–24 reports that Mary brought the two birds.
Inspection makes time part of the decision

The priest here works as an inspector, and the chapter gives him tests. He checks hair color, depth, and spread (verses 3–8). When the signs are unclear, verse 4 orders a seven-day wait. Verse 5 orders a second look and, if needed, a second wait. So no one is sent out of the camp on a first glance. Verse 46 shows why care matters: the unclean person must live alone outside.
Return from separation includes provision for limited means

Chapter 13 sent the sick person outside the camp. Chapter 14 is about the way back. The priest goes out to meet him (verse 3). The return happens in steps: outside, into the camp, into the tent, to the altar. Verse 21 makes sure cost does not block the last step. A poor person brings one lamb, not three, and two birds. The closing words are the same for rich and poor: “he shall be clean.”
Ordinary bodily conditions affect access to sacred space

The chapter covers things that happen to healthy bodies and to sick ones. It treats men first (verses 2–18) and women second (verses 19–30). Most cases need only washing and waiting until evening. None is called a crime. Verse 31 gives the reason for all of it: God’s tabernacle is “among them.” Because he lives in the camp, the people’s bodily states matter near his tent. The rules manage access to that tent and say nothing about a person’s worth.
The annual rite addresses the sanctuary as well as the people

Verse 16 says atonement is made “for the Holy Place.” The reason is the people’s uncleanness and all their sins. The tent stands in the middle of the camp, so their wrongs reach it. Once a year the room, the tent, and the altar are cleansed (verse 20). Then the people’s sins are confessed over a goat and carried away (verses 21–22). The day clears both the place and the people. Verse 30 states the result: “You shall be clean from all your sins.”
Blood receives a stated meaning within the ritual system

The ban on eating blood appeared in Genesis 9:4 and Leviticus 3:17. Verse 11 is where the reason is given. Blood stands for the animal’s life. God says he has “given it to you on the altar” for atonement. So blood has one proper use, and it is not food. Verse 13 applies this even to wild game that is never offered. The hunter pours the blood out and covers it, treating the life with respect.
The land becomes part of the warning about conduct

Most of the chapter concerns people who live in one large household. Verses 6–18 name mothers, sisters, granddaughters, aunts, and daughters-in-law. Each rule is addressed to the one who would approach, so the relative is protected. Verses 24–25 widen the view to the land itself. Canaan’s people defiled it, and it “vomited out her inhabitants.” Verse 28 gives Israel the same warning, with no special protection.
Holiness reaches the marketplace

The chapter opens with “You shall be holy” (verse 2). It then spends most of its length on fields, wages, courts, and trade. Verse 36 ends the list at the scale: just balances, weights, and measures. A false weight cheats a buyer; the trade weight shown is that kind of tool. The verse ends with the exodus: “who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” So honest trade is part of belonging to the God who freed them. The same chapter holds “love your neighbor as yourself” (verse 18).
Distinct identity comes with threats of exclusion and death

Chapter 18 listed forbidden acts. Chapter 20 attaches penalties, and many are death. Verses 2–5 begin with child sacrifice to Molech and blame neighbors who look away. Verses 22–23 give the reason: other nations did these things and lost the land. Verse 24 sets the promise beside the threat. Israel will inherit a good land and has been separated from the peoples. Verse 26 says what the separation is for: “that you should be mine.”
A limit on priestly service does not remove every priestly share

Verses 17–21 bar a priest with a bodily defect from offering at the altar. The same standard was set for the animals offered there (1:3). Verse 22 follows at once with what he keeps. He eats “the bread of his God,” both the holy and the most holy. That food was the priests’ living (6:16–18). So the limit is on one task, not on his place among the priests. The text does not call him unclean or sinful.
An offering rule also limits how an animal family is treated

Most of this chapter is about what makes an offering acceptable. Verses 27–28 add two limits that concern the animals themselves. A newborn stays with its mother for seven days. A mother and her young are not killed on the same day. The text gives no reason. The effect is to keep mother and young in view. Even at the altar, the animal’s life is given some regard.
The festival calendar includes people without their own harvest

Verses 4–21 and 23–44 are a calendar of feasts and offerings. Verse 22 interrupts it with a rule about reaping. It comes right after the harvest feast of verses 15–21. The farmer who brings loaves to God must leave grain in the field. The poor and the foreigner have no harvest of their own to celebrate. The rule repeats 19:9–10 almost word for word. So the feast is not complete if the harvest is kept only for the owner.
A single legal standard stands beside a severe public judgment

The man in this case has an Egyptian father (verse 10). The people wait for the LORD’s word before acting (verse 12). The ruling does not rest on his mixed family. Verse 16 says a foreigner or a native-born person gets the same penalty. Verse 22 states it as a rule: “one kind of law” for both. The same verses limit payback to the harm done: eye for eye, no more. The sentence is severe, and the text reports that it was carried out (verse 23).
Land ownership has limits

Verse 23 gives the reason behind the whole chapter. The land belongs to the LORD, and Israel lives on it as his guests. So a sale is really a lease of crops until the Jubilee (verses 15–16). A family that falls into debt gets its field back in the fiftieth year. Verse 42 says the same of people: Israelites are God’s servants, not slaves. The chapter does not extend that rule to foreigners (verses 44–46). Its limit on wealth protects Israel’s own families from permanent loss.
The warnings do not end with rejection in exile

The warnings come in five stages (verses 16, 18, 21, 23, 27). Each stage is a chance to turn back before the next. The last stage is exile in an enemy’s land. Verse 44 begins “Yet for all that.” Even there God will not destroy them utterly or break his covenant. The reason given is his name: “for I am the LORD their God.” Verses 40–42 say what opens the way back: confession and a humbled heart.
A vow requires rules for people who cannot meet the valuation

Verses 3–7 set fixed values for people who have been vowed. A fixed scale is simple, but it can be out of reach. Verse 8 handles that case. The priest sets a value “according to his ability to pay.” So a vow made in faith does not become a debt that crushes. The same care appeared in 5:7, 12:8, and 14:21. Leviticus ends as it began, making room for people with less.
